name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q01 - Decreasing order of boiling points of alkanes

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following in decreasing order of their boiling points.

(A) \(n\)-butane
(B) 2-methylbutane
(C) \(n\)-pentane
(D) 2,2-dimethylpropane

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In alkanes, boiling point depends on intermolecular van der Waals forces, which increase with molecular mass (chain length) and surface area.

Step 2: Evaluation of Molecular Mass
Among the given alkanes, \(n\)-butane has four carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}\)), whereas \(n\)-pentane, 2-methylbutane, and 2,2-dimethylpropane are isomeric pentanes with five carbon atoms (\(\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}\)). Therefore, \(n\)-butane has the lowest boiling point.

Step 3: Effect of Branching
Among isomeric pentanes, branching makes the molecule more compact and spherical, decreasing the surface area and weakening intermolecular van der Waals forces. Thus, the boiling point decreases with increasing branching: \(n\)-pentane (unbranched) > 2-methylbutane (one branch) > 2,2-dimethylpropane (two branches).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of boiling points is \(\mathrm{C} > \mathrm{B} > \mathrm{D} > \mathrm{A}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q02 - Increasing order of halogen reactivity with alkanes

questiontext.text: Arrange the halogens \(\mathrm{F}_2\), \(\mathrm{Cl}_2\), \(\mathrm{Br}_2\), \(\mathrm{I}_2\), in order of their increasing reactivity with alkanes.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogenation of alkanes proceeds via a free-radical substitution mechanism. The reactivity of halogens depends on the thermodynamics and activation energy of the propagation steps, particularly hydrogen abstraction.

Step 2: Evaluation
As we move down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine, the electronegativity and oxidizing power of the halogen decrease, and the \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond formed becomes weaker. Consequently, the reaction becomes less exothermic (and even endothermic for iodine).

Step 3: Application
Fluorine reacts explosively even in the dark, chlorine reacts rapidly in diffused sunlight, bromine reacts slowly and requires heating or UV light, and iodine reacts very slowly and reversibly.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of reactivity of halogens with alkanes is \(\mathrm{I}_2 < \mathrm{Br}_2 < \mathrm{Cl}_2 < \mathrm{F}_2\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q03 - Reduction order of alkyl halides with zinc

questiontext.text: The increasing order of reduction of alkyl halides with zinc and dilute \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Reduction of alkyl halides (\(\mathrm{R-X}\)) with zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid involves cleavage of the carbon-halogen (\(\mathrm{C-X}\)) bond to form an alkane (\(\mathrm{R-H}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
The ease of cleavage of the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond depends inversely on the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond dissociation enthalpy. As the size of the halogen atom increases from chlorine to bromine to iodine, the \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond length increases and the bond strength decreases.

Step 3: Application
Since the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is the weakest and the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond is the strongest among \(\mathrm{R-Cl}\), \(\mathrm{R-Br}\), and \(\mathrm{R-I}\), \(\mathrm{R-I}\) undergoes reduction most readily while \(\mathrm{R-Cl}\) is reduced most slowly.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The increasing order of reduction of alkyl halides with zinc and dilute \(\mathrm{HCl}\) is \(\mathrm{R - Cl} < \mathrm{R - Br} < \mathrm{R - I}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q04 - Correct IUPAC name of branched alkane

questiontext.text: The correct IUPAC name of the following alkane is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The given structural formula is a saturated branched alkane containing an 8-carbon longest continuous chain with substituent groups.

Step 2: Conventions and Rules
According to IUPAC nomenclature rules: (1) Select the longest continuous carbon chain; when two chains of equal length compete, choose the one with the greater number of substituents. (2) Number the chain to give the substituents the lowest possible locant set. (3) List substituents in alphabetical order, ignoring multiplicative prefixes such as di-.

Step 3: Relevant Principles
Longest chain selection and lowest locant rule for branched alkanes.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Starting from the terminal methyl carbon of the isopropyl-like branch on the left and moving through the main horizontal chain to the right gives an 8-carbon parent chain (octane) bearing three substituents: a methyl group at position 2, an ethyl group at position 3, and an ethyl group at position 6. Numbering from the opposite end would give locants 3, 6, 7, which is higher than 2, 3, 6. Arranging ethyl before methyl alphabetically gives 3,6-Diethyl-2-methyloctane.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The locant set (2, 3, 6) is minimal and the chain has the maximum number of substituents (three). The correct IUPAC name is 3,6-Diethyl-2-methyloctane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q05 - Addition of HBr to 1-butene products

questiontext.text:
The addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to 1-butene gives a mixture of products A, B and C

(A)   (B)   (C)

The mixture consists of

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
1-Butene (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH=CH_2}\)) reacts with \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to yield three products: A and B (two enantiomeric forms of 2-bromobutane) and C (1-bromobutane).

Step 2: Assumptions and Principles
In the absence of peroxides, the electrophilic addition of \(\mathrm{HBr}\) to an unsymmetrical alkene follows Markovnikov's rule via the more stable carbocation intermediate.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Markovnikov's rule: protonation of the double bond occurs to form the more stable secondary carbocation (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H-CH_3}\)) rather than the less stable primary carbocation (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2-\overset{+}{C}H_2}\)).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
The secondary carbocation is planar (\(sp^2\) hybridized), so the bromide ion (\(\mathrm{Br^-}\)) can attack equally from either face, producing a racemic mixture of the two enantiomers of 2-bromobutane (products A and B) as the major products. Attack on the minor primary carbocation pathway gives 1-bromobutane (product C) as the minor product.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the mixture consists of A and B as major products and C as minor product.

answer.text: A and B as major and C as minor products
B as major, A and C as minor products
B as minor, A and C as major products
A and B as minor and C as major products

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q06 - Alkene not showing geometrical isomerism

questiontext.text: Which of the following will not show geometrical isomerism?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For an alkene (\(\mathrm{abC=Ccd}\)) to exhibit geometrical (cis-trans or \(E\text{-}Z\)) isomerism, each of the two doubly bonded carbon atoms must be attached to two different groups or atoms (that is, \(\mathrm{a} \neq \mathrm{b}\) and \(\mathrm{c} \neq \mathrm{d}\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Checking each alkene structure:
- \(\mathrm{F(Cl)C=C(H)D}\): one carbon has \(\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\); the other has \(\mathrm{H}\) and \(\mathrm{D}\). Both carbons have two different groups, so it shows geometrical isomerism.
- \(\mathrm{F(Cl)C=C(F)Cl}\): each carbon has \(\mathrm{F}\) and \(\mathrm{Cl}\) (two different groups), so it shows geometrical isomerism.
- \(\mathrm{H_3C(C_2H_5)C=C(C_2H_5)CH_3}\): each carbon has \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{C_2H_5}\) (two different groups), so it shows geometrical isomerism.
- \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=C(CH_3)C_2H_5}\): the left doubly bonded carbon is attached to two identical methyl (\(\mathrm{CH_3}\)) groups.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Because one of the doubly bonded carbon atoms carries two identical \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) groups, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=C(CH_3)C_2H_5}\) will not show geometrical isomerism.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q07 - Decreasing reactivity of hydrogen halides with propene

questiontext.text: Arrange the following hydrogen halides in order of their decreasing reactivity with propene.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The addition of hydrogen halides (\(\mathrm{HX}\)) to propene is an electrophilic addition reaction in which the rate-determining step involves protonation of the double bond by \(\mathrm{HX}\) to form a carbocation intermediate.

Step 2: Evaluation
The ease of donation of a proton (\(\mathrm{H^+}\)) depends on the \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond dissociation energy. Down the halogen group, the atomic size increases, so the \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond length increases and the bond dissociation energy decreases (\(\mathrm{H-Cl} > \mathrm{H-Br} > \mathrm{H-I}\)).

Step 3: Application
Because \(\mathrm{HI}\) has the weakest \(\mathrm{H-X}\) bond and is the strongest acid among the three, it protonates propene most readily, followed by \(\mathrm{HBr}\) and then \(\mathrm{HCl}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of reactivity of hydrogen halides with propene is \(\mathrm{HI} > \mathrm{HBr} > \mathrm{HCl}\).

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following carbanions in order of their decreasing stability.

(A) \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C} - \mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{C}^{-}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{H} - \mathrm{C}\equiv \mathrm{C}^{-}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_2^{-}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbanion stability increases with increasing electronegativity (higher \(s\)-character) of the negatively charged carbon atom and decreases with electron-donating (\(+I\)) groups attached to it.

Step 2: Evaluation
In \(\mathrm{H}-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{C}^{-}\) (B) and \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{C}^{-}\) (A), the negatively charged carbon is \(sp\)-hybridized (\(50\%\) \(s\)-character), whereas in \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{CH}_2^{-}\) (C), it is \(sp^3\)-hybridized (\(25\%\) \(s\)-character). Because \(sp\)-hybridized carbon is much more electronegative, it accommodates the negative charge much better than \(sp^3\)-hybridized carbon, making A and B far more stable than C.

Step 3: Application
Comparing A and B, the methyl group in \(\mathrm{H}_3\mathrm{C}-\mathrm{C}\equiv\mathrm{C}^{-}\) exerts an electron-donating \(+I\) effect, which intensifies the negative charge on the acetylide carbon and destabilizes A relative to B.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of carbanion stability is \(\mathrm{B} > \mathrm{A} > \mathrm{C}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q09 - Rate of beta-elimination of alkyl halides

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following alkyl halides in decreasing order of the rate of \(\beta\)-elimination reaction with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\).

(A) \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\underset{\mathrm{CH}_3}{\overset{\mathrm{H}}{\mathrm{C}}}-\mathrm{CH}_2\mathrm{Br}\)
(B) \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Br}\)
(C) \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{Br}\)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Dehydrohalogenation (\(\beta\)-elimination) of primary alkyl halides with alcoholic \(\mathrm{KOH}\) proceeds via an \(\mathrm{E2}\) mechanism. The rate of elimination increases with the stability of the alkene formed in the transition state (Zaitsev/Saytzeff rule).

Step 2: Evaluation
The alkene products obtained from the three alkyl halides are:
- From A (\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH-CH_2Br}\)): 2-methylpropene, \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2C=CH_2}\) (disubstituted alkene, 6 \(\alpha\)-hydrogens).
- From C (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2-CH_2Br}\)): propene, \(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH_2}\) (monosubstituted alkene, 3 \(\alpha\)-hydrogens).
- From B (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH_2Br}\)): ethene, \(\mathrm{CH_2=CH_2}\) (unsubstituted alkene, 0 \(\alpha\)-hydrogens).

Step 3: Application
Greater hyperconjugation (more \(\alpha\)-hydrogens) stabilizes the forming double bond in the transition state, lowering the activation energy and increasing the rate of elimination.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The decreasing order of the rate of \(\beta\)-elimination is \(\mathrm{A} > \mathrm{C} > \mathrm{B}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q10 - Incomplete combustion reaction of methane

questiontext.text: Which of the following reactions of methane is incomplete combustion:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Combustion of alkanes in a limited (insufficient) supply of air or dioxygen leads to incomplete combustion, producing carbon black (\(\mathrm{C(s)}\)) or carbon monoxide along with water.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Catalytic oxidation of methane with \(\mathrm{O_2}\) over \(\mathrm{Cu}\) at \(523\ \mathrm{K}\) and \(100\ \mathrm{atm}\) to form \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\), and over \(\mathrm{Mo_2O_3}\) to form \(\mathrm{HCHO}\), are controlled oxidation reactions.
- Oxidation of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) with \(2\mathrm{O_2}\) to \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\) is complete combustion.
- Reaction of \(\mathrm{CH_4}\) with limited \(\mathrm{O_2}\) to yield solid carbon (\(\mathrm{C(s)}\)) and \(\mathrm{H_2O(l)}\) is incomplete combustion.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The reaction \(\mathrm{CH}_4 + \mathrm{O}_2 \longrightarrow \mathrm{C(s)} + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O(l)}\) represents incomplete combustion of methane.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q11 - Controlled oxidation reactions of methane

questiontext.text: Some oxidation reactions of methane are given below. Which of them is/are controlled oxidation reactions?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Controlled oxidation of alkanes involves heating them with a regulated supply of dioxygen or air at high pressure and in the presence of suitable catalysts to obtain useful oxygenated organic compounds such as alcohols or aldehydes.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{CH}_4(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CO}_2(\mathrm{g}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\) is complete combustion.
- \(\mathrm{CH}_4(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{C}(\mathrm{s}) + 2\mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}(\mathrm{l})\) is incomplete combustion.
- \(\mathrm{CH}_4(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Mo}_2\mathrm{O}_3} \mathrm{HCHO} + \mathrm{H}_2\mathrm{O}\) is controlled catalytic oxidation to methanal.
- \(2\mathrm{CH}_4(\mathrm{g}) + \mathrm{O}_2(\mathrm{g}) \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Cu}/523/100\ \mathrm{atm}} 2\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH}\) is controlled catalytic oxidation to methanol.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both catalytic reactions yielding methanal (\(\mathrm{HCHO}\)) and methanol (\(\mathrm{CH}_3\mathrm{OH}\)) are controlled oxidation reactions.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q13 - Correct IUPAC names of substituted decane

questiontext.text:
Which are the correct IUPAC names of the following compound?

\[\begin{array}{c} \mathrm{HC(CH_3)_2} \\ | \\ \mathrm{H_3C-CH_2-CH_2-CH-CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3} \\ | \\ \mathrm{H_3C-CH-CH_2CH_3} \end{array}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The given branched alkane has a 10-carbon continuous horizontal chain (decane) bearing two branched alkyl substituents on adjacent carbons.

Step 2: Conventions and Rules
Number the decane chain from the end nearest to the substituents to obtain the lowest locant set. Both trivial (sec-butyl, iso-propyl) and systematic (1-methylpropyl, 1-methylethyl) substituent names are accepted in IUPAC nomenclature, with alphabetical ordering applied to the substituent names.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
Numbering from the left gives locants 4 and 5 (instead of 6 and 7 from the right). At C-4, the substituent is \(\mathrm{-CH(CH_3)_2}\), which is named \(\text{iso-propyl}\) or \(\text{1-methylethyl}\). At C-5, the substituent is \(\mathrm{-CH(CH_3)CH_2CH_3}\), which is named \(\text{sec-butyl}\) or \(\text{1-methylpropyl}\). Using trivial substituent names (ignoring the italicized prefix \(\text{sec-}\), so 'b' comes before 'i'), the name is 5-sec-Butyl-4-iso-propyldecane. Using systematic names ('methylethyl' comes before 'methylpropyl' alphabetically), the name is 4-(1-methylethyl)-5-(1-methylpropyl)-decane.

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Both 5-sec-Butyl-4-iso-propyldecane and 4-(1-methylethyl)-5-(1-methylpropyl)-decane are correct IUPAC names.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q14 - Correct IUPAC names of neopentyldecane

questiontext.text:
Which are the correct IUPAC names of the following compound?

\[\begin{array}{c} \mathrm{H_3C-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_2-CH_3} \\ | \\ \mathrm{CH_2} \\ | \\ \mathrm{H_3C-C-CH_3} \\ | \\ \mathrm{CH_3} \end{array}\]

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The given branched alkane has a 10-carbon horizontal chain (decane) with a 5-carbon branched substituent attached at the middle.

Step 2: Conventions and Rules
Select the longest continuous carbon chain and number it to give the substituent the lowest possible locant. Both the trivial prefix \(\text{neo-pentyl}\) and the systematic complex substituent name \(\text{2',2'-dimethylpropyl}\) are valid in IUPAC nomenclature.

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
The longest continuous chain has 10 carbons (decane). Numbering from the left gives the substituent at position 5 (which is lower than position 6 from the right). The substituent \(\mathrm{-CH_2-C(CH_3)_3}\) has a 3-carbon main chain (propyl) with two methyl groups at C-2' of the side chain, so it is systematically named \(\text{2',2'-dimethylpropyl}\) and trivially named \(\text{neo-pentyl}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Answer
Both 5-(2',2'-Dimethylpropyl)-decane and 5-neo-Pentyldecane are correct IUPAC names.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q15 - Directive influence of halogen in benzene

questiontext.text: For an electrophilic substitution reaction, the presence of a halogen atom in the benzene ring

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Halogen atoms attached to a benzene ring exhibit two opposing electronic effects: a strong electron-withdrawing inductive effect (\(-I\)) due to high electronegativity, and a weaker electron-donating resonance effect (\(+R\) / \(+M\)) via lone-pair donation into the \(\pi\)-system.

Step 2: Evaluation
- Because the \(-I\) effect dominates over the \(+R\) effect, the overall electron density of the benzene ring decreases, deactivating the ring towards electrophilic substitution.
- However, the \(+R\) effect delocalizes lone-pair electrons specifically to the ortho and para positions, increasing the charge density at the ortho and para positions relative to the meta position.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Thus, a halogen atom deactivates the benzene ring by inductive effect and increases the charge density at ortho and para positions relative to the meta position by resonance.

answer.text: increases the charge density at ortho and para position relative to meta position by resonance
directs the incoming electrophile to meta position by increasing the charge density relative to ortho and para position.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q16 - Effect of nitro group in nitrobenzene

questiontext.text: In an electrophilic substitution reaction of nitrobenzene, the presence of nitro group

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The nitro group (\(\mathrm{-NO_2}\)) is a strongly electron-withdrawing group exhibiting both a negative inductive effect (\(-I\)) and a negative resonance effect (\(-R\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
- By the \(-I\) effect, the \(\mathrm{-NO_2}\) group withdraws electron density from the benzene ring, deactivating it towards electrophilic attack.
- By the \(-R\) effect, it draws \(\pi\)-electrons out of the ring, placing positive charges at the ortho and para positions in the resonance hybrids. This decreases the charge density at the ortho and para positions relative to the meta position, making the meta position comparatively less deactivated.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The nitro group deactivates the ring by inductive effect and decreases the charge density at the ortho and para positions relative to the meta position by resonance.

answer.text: decreases the charge density at ortho and para position of the ring relative to meta position by resonance.
increases the charge density at meta position relative to the ortho and para positions of the ring by resonance.

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Carbocation stability is enhanced by resonance delocalization of the positive charge (including lone-pair resonance from adjacent heteroatoms and \(\pi\)-bond conjugation) as well as hyperconjugation and \(+I\) effects.

Step 2: Evaluation
- \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{CH}_2^{\oplus}\) is strongly stabilized by resonance donation of a lone pair from oxygen (\(\mathrm{CH_3-\overset{+}{O}=CH_2}\)), giving every atom an octet, so it is much more stable than \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2^{\oplus}\).
- \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_2CH^\oplus}\) is a secondary carbocation (6 \(\alpha\)-hydrogens), which is more stable—not less stable—than the primary carbocation \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2^\oplus\) (2 \(\alpha\)-hydrogens).
- \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2^\oplus\) (allyl carbocation) is resonance-stabilized, making it more stable than the primary propyl carbocation \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2^\oplus\).
- \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}^\oplus\) (vinyl carbocation) has the positive charge on a more electronegative \(sp^2\)-hybridized carbon and is less stable than \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2^\oplus\).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct statements are that \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{O}-\mathrm{CH}_2^{\oplus}\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2^{\oplus}\) and that \(\mathrm{CH}_2=\mathrm{CH}-\mathrm{CH}_2^\oplus\) is more stable than \(\mathrm{CH}_3-\mathrm{CH}_2-\mathrm{CH}_2^\oplus\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_HYDROCARBONS_MCQ_Q19 - Molecules having non-zero dipole moment

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A molecule has a non-zero net dipole moment when its individual bond dipoles do not cancel each other due to molecular symmetry.

Step 2: Evaluation
- 2,2-Dimethylpropane (\(\mathrm{C(CH_3)_4}\)) is tetrahedral and completely symmetrical, so its bond dipoles cancel out (\(\mu = 0\)).
- \(\text{trans}\)-Pent-2-ene (\(\mathrm{CH_3-CH=CH-C_2H_5}\)) has two different alkyl groups (\(\mathrm{-CH_3}\) and \(\mathrm{-C_2H_5}\)) on opposite sides of the double bond; because their inductive/bond dipoles are unequal, they do not cancel completely (\(\mu \neq 0\)).
- \(\text{cis}\)-Hex-3-ene (\(\mathrm{C_2H_5-CH=CH-C_2H_5}\)) has both ethyl groups on the same side of the double bond, so their bond dipoles add up to give a net dipole moment (\(\mu \neq 0\)).
- 2,2,3,3-Tetramethylbutane (\(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3C-C(CH_3)_3}\)) is symmetrical, so its dipole moment is zero.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The molecules having a dipole moment are \(\text{trans}\)-Pent-2-ene and \(\text{cis}\)-Hex-3-ene.
